Tufailur Rahman with Md Delwar Hossain Khan, Advocates — For the Petitioner.
MA Wahab Miah with Faisal Hossain Khan, Advocates — For the Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Shamsuddin Ahmed ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Dalil Patan and others ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment: 8. It is claimed by opposite party No. 1 that the suit property measuring 0.13 decimals of land belonged to the late Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee who was an Advocate of the Kishoreganj Bar Association. The deceased defendant-appellant-petitioner denies the claim of opposite party No.1 that the suit property exclusively belonged to the late Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee. According to him, the suit property was acquired in the name of the ''Karla'' of the family with the income of Hindu joint family property. The deceased defendant-appellant-petitioner claims that he purchased the suit land in his name and also in the names of his wife and sons by kabalas from Ajoy Kumar Bhattacharjee in the year 1978. Exts. B, B(1), B(2) and B(3) are the kabalas of the deceased defendant-appellant-petitioner. Exts. C, D, D(1) and E are the receipts showing payment of rent and Municipal Taxes by the deceased defendant-appellant-petitioner. Ext. G(1) is certified copy of the order passed in Other Class Suit No.279 of 1969 filed by Ajoy Kumar Bhattacharjee against the then Government of East Pakistan. It appears from Ext. G(1) that a temporary injunction was issued against the then Government of East Pakistan restraining them from evicting Ajoy Kumar Bhattacharjee from the suit land otherwise than under the due process of law. Ext. G(2) is the certified copy of the plaint of Other Class Suit No. 215 of 1974 filed by Ajoy Kumar Bhattacharjee and another for declaration of their right and title to the suit land. The said suit appears to have been instituted against the heirs of late Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee. The above suit appears to have been decreed ex parte (vide certified copy of the order Ext.G(3). In the face of all these documents it can not be said that Ajoy Kumar Bhattacharjee had no interest in the suit land. It is true that both the learned Courts below concurrently had arrived at some decisions on facts. It is true at the same time that this Court under its revisional jurisdiction can interfere if the facts leading to the evidence are found to be perverse based on misreading of the same. Both the learned Courts below appear to have altogether overlooked the evidence on record, documentary as well as oral. Both the learned Courts below particularly the learned appellate Court has spent much time on the case as made out by the deceased defendant-appellant-petitioner as if it was his case and not that of opposite party No. 1. It is the settled principle of law that failure or success of the plaintiff depends upon the strength of his own case and not upon the weakness of the defendant''s case. The learned appellate Court below, it further appears, has been out to find out loopholes and weaknesses in the defendant''s case. It transpires that both the learned Courts below have been labouring under a misconception that since the plaintiff has initiated the proceeding his case should be viewed favourably. The learned Courts below have totally ignored the background of the case vis-a-vis the alleged transfer of a town property measuring 0.13 decimals of land with pucca and other structures standing thereon for a paltry sum of Taka 4,000.00 only. Ext. 1 i.e. the deed of agreement of sale is of the year 1963. But opposite party No. 1 instituted the instant suit on 28-8-71 i.e. in the thick of the liberation war, though there is stipulation in Ext.1 that the vendor would execute and register the kabala within 3 years from the date of its execution. The contesting deceased defendant-appellant-petitioner specifically has asserted that Ext. 1 is a forged, collusive, bogus and ante-dated document for the purpose of grabbing a valuable town property belonging to a renowned lawyer having good practice at the Bar. It is further asserted by him that Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee, the alleged vendor of the suit land, left for Calcutta in the year 1965 or before for his treatment there and ultimately he breathed his last in Calcutta. There was an obiturary reference on 24-3-65 at the Kishoreganj Bar Association condoling his death. Ext.I is the resolution adopted at the Kishoreganj Bar Association condoling the death of Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee . It is contended by the contesting deceased defendant-appellant-petitioner that Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee having died and a condolence resolution having been taken on 24-3-65, the story of his acceptance of the balance amount of the consideration money of Taka 1,000.00 on 1-9-1968 as shown on the back of Ext.1 is a myth. It appears from the judgment and decree of the learned Courts below that they attached no value to this important and vital piece of documentary evidence. They seem to have raised irrelevant questions with a view to down-grading the evidentiary value of Ext.1 when the resolution condoling the death of Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee was taken on 24-3-1965 conclusive presumption becomes irresistible that Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee died in 1965 or in the later part of 1964. There is no room for doubt regarding the death of Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee in the year 1964 or in 1965. The reasons advanced by the learned Courts below that Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee lived till 1-5-1968 to receive the balance amount of the consideration money of Taka 1,000.00 are not at all acceptable. I have full reliance upon the authenticity and evidentiary value of Ext. 1. This being the position the story of Jogendra Chandra Bhattacharjee's acceptance of the balance amount of the consideration money of Taka 1,000.00 from the opposite party No.1 on 1-9-1968 has no legs to stand upon. This aspect of opposite party No. 1''s case has thus fallen through, the genuineness and authenticity of Ext. 1 becomes a big question mark. The learned Court below should have found out that the stamps of Ext. 1 were purchased 6 months before the execution of the alleged deed of agreement of sale. Doubt naturally arises as to why the opposite-party No. 1 should purchase stamps 6 months before the execution of Ext. 1. I have no manner of doubt to hold that Ext. 1 is anything but a genuine document. That it is not an authentic and genuine document has been highlighted by Ext. 1.
